title: Questions & Answers on the AI Act

covered_actors: Public and private actors inside and outside the EU placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market or putting them into service or use in the EU
Providers of general-purpose AI models (including models with systemic risks)
Public authorities and private operators providing public services
prohibited_practices: Exploitation of vulnerabilities of persons, manipulation, and use of subliminal techniques
Social scoring for public and private purposes
Individual predictive policing based solely on profiling people
Untargeted scraping of internet or CCTV for facial images to build up or expand facial recognition databases
Emotion recognition in the workplace and education institutions (unless for medical or safety reasons)
Biometric categorisation of natural persons to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, or sexual orientation
Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes (subject to narrow exceptions)

compliance_deadlines: 2025-02-02: Prohibitions, definitions, and AI literacy provisions apply
2025-08-02: Governance rules and obligations for general-purpose AI models apply

2026-08-02: General application date of the AI Act (2 years after entry into force), including Article 50 transparency obligations and Annex III high-risk AI system rules (subject to proposed adjustment under the Digital Omnibus proposal)
2027-08-02: Obligations for high-risk AI systems embedded in regulated products listed in Annex II apply (36 months after entry into force)
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Member States must set effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties with thresholds of up to €35m or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for prohibited practices or data requirement non-compliance; up to €15m or 3% of worldwide annual turnover for other AI Act obligations (and for European Commission fines on general-purpose AI model providers); and up to €7.5m or 1.5% of worldwide annual turnover for supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities. For SMEs, the lower of the two amounts applies. The EDPS is empowered to impose fines on non-compliant EU institutions, agencies, or bodies.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: This document is an explanatory European Commission Q&A webpage (last updated 28 January 2026) summarizing the EU AI Act rather than the enacted statutory text itself. Pre-release R&D/prototyping activities and AI systems exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes are exempt from the Act. Delays in CEN/CENELEC harmonised standards beyond August 2025 led the Commission to introduce the Digital Omnibus proposal (19 November 2025) to link high-risk application timelines to the availability of standards, common specifications, or guidelines. Implementation is supported by voluntary tools including the GPAI Code of Practice, an upcoming Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content, the AI Pact, the AI Act Service Desk, and the Single Information Platform (SIP).

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The document frames the EU AI Act primarily around fundamental rights, anchoring prohibitions, high-risk classifications, anti-bias duties, biometric restrictions, and impact assessments in EU values, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, non-discrimination, privacy, democracy, and the rule of law. Fundamental rights edges out consumer and public safety (which is prominent in product-safety, physical-safety, and anti-deception rationales) and innovation enablement (which emphasizes trust, internal-market harmonisation, regulatory sandboxes, and proportionate rules) because rights protection recurs as the foundational legal rationale across nearly every substantive section of the Q&A. Economic competitiveness (global leadership, growth, and EU industrial strength) and existential/catastrophic risk (CBRN attacks, large-scale cyberattacks, and loss of human control from systemic-risk GPAI models) appear as explicit secondary justifications, while misinformation and strategic distortion of beliefs provide only minor social-stability framing. National security is explicitly carved out as an exemption rather than a governance rationale, and employment mentions lack workforce-transition or reskilling framing.
